presentation:
A 58-year-old woman was referred for a 6-month history of progressive hoarseness and dysphagia, associated with a 20-lb weight loss. Over the preceding year, she had right hand and lower limb pain and weakness; she was diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome and C6, C7, and L5 radiculopathies. Four months before presentation, she had right middle lobe pneumonia treated with antibiotics. A thoracic CT scan at that time showed right middle lobe consolidation, atelectasis, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy; bronchoalveolar lavage, brush biopsies, and endobronchial biopsies were negative for malignancy, and her vocal cords were documented as normal. A follow-up CT demonstrated moderate resolution of the pneumonia.

Her history included a 40–pack-year smoking history and COPD, with no prior head or neck surgery. On examination, she appeared cachectic with audible inspiratory stridor and increased work of breathing. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy revealed bilateral vocal cord paralysis. There was no palpable neck mass, and the remainder of the cranial nerve and head and neck examinations were normal. After tracheostomy, a CT scan from the skull base to the aortic arch showed no lesion along the course of either vagus nerve. A modified barium swallow demonstrated mild oral and moderate pharyngeal dysphagia with frank aspiration, and enteral feeding was initiated.
reasoning_trace:
1. Iatrogenic injury considered and excluded — “There was no previous history of head and neck surgery.”  
2. Direct tumour compression considered and excluded — “No lesion along the course of either vagus nerve was found.”  
3. Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy considered and excluded — “The study did not demonstrate hallmarks of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (namely, conduction block or temporal dispersion).”  
4. Idiopathic bilateral vocal cord paralysis remained a possibility but imaging prompted evaluation for rarer causes — “…the Otolaryngologist must broaden his/her differential diagnosis and consider more infrequent causes before concluding that BVCP is idiopathic.”  
5. Paraneoplastic neuropathy suspected with evolving polyneuropathy and dysphagia, confirmed by anti-Hu antibody positivity — “An anti-paraneoplastic antibody panel was positive for anti-Hu antibodies.”

presentation: A 12-year-old boy with a history of ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement and chronic, nonprogressive encephalopathy secondary to neonatal pneumococcal meningitis presents with headache and a dystonic posture of the upper limb. He has known spastic tetraparesis and epilepsy. On examination he is alert and oriented; no signs of shunt malfunction are seen on noncontrast head CT. Brain MRI shows a cystic lesion in the anterior cervical canal; subsequent cervical spine MRI confirms an intradural extramedullary cyst extending from C2 to C4, with T2- and T1-weighted signal identical to CSF, consistent with an acquired arachnoid cyst, and with distal cord swelling and increased T2 signal below C4 suggestive of compressive myelopathy. He is started on oral dexamethasone and ketorolac. Four days later, posterior cervical decompression and cyst fenestration are performed uneventfully. Immediately after surgery, he has right arm monoplegia. Postsurgical MRI on the same day shows a marked increase in the extent of intramedullary, predominantly central, T2 hyperintensity from C2 through C7–T1, without contrast enhancement on T1-weighted images.
reasoning_trace:
1. Iatrogenic cord injury — “The surgical history in addition to the imaging follow up can help to discard an iatrogenic injury.”  
2. Postsurgical hematoma — “A postsurgical hematoma is easily recognizable in the MRI scan.”  
3. Ischemia by hypoperfusion — “Ischemia by hypoperfusion ... should be ruled out. Diffusion-weighted imaging sequence can be useful to perform the differential diagnosis with ischemia.”  
4. Demyelinating disorder — “Any undiagnosed demyelinating disorder should be ruled out. The clinical history and the study of the brain with MRI could help to rule out a demyelinating disease.”

presentation: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, with no significant medical history, was admitted at 36 weeks of gestation for severe preeclampsia and rapidly progressive vulvar swelling. She was apyretic, and there was no history of trauma, infection, or topical medication use. Blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg, and urine dipstick showed 3+ proteinuria. Examination of the external genitalia revealed massive edema of the labia minora and majora, predominantly on the left side, with fissuring of the inner aspect of the right labia majora and a serous discharge. Obstetrical examination showed a tense uterus, a closed cervix, intact membranes, and cephalic presentation. Continuous fetal monitoring demonstrated a flat heart-rate pattern without accelerations. There were no signs of lower-limb thrombosis or regional lymphadenopathy, and only mild pedal edema. Because of suspected retroplacental hematoma, a cesarean delivery was performed, yielding a female infant weighing 2500 g with Apgar scores of 10 and 10. Initial laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, a normal platelet count, normal prothrombin level and liver transaminases, a negative infectious workup, serum protein of 21 g/L, and 24-hour proteinuria of 4 g.
reasoning_trace:
1. Tocolysis-related edema considered — “Massive vulvar edema has been reported in the literature after tocolysis…”  
2. Vulvovaginitis considered — “…after … vulvovaginitis…”  
3. Crohn’s disease considered — “…after … Crohn’s disease…”  
4. Local trauma, infections, and vascular or lymphatic obstruction excluded — “Other possible causes of vulvar edema are local trauma, infections and vascular and lymphatic obstructions. None of these could be observed in our patient.”  
5. Hypoproteinemia in severe preeclampsia identified as cause — “The vulvar edema in our patient was probably due to hypoprotidemia which is quite often associated with severe pre-eclampsia.”

presentation: An 8-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of erythema, scaling, sticky yellow discharge, and patchy hair loss on his frontal scalp. His symptoms worsened despite brief courses of cephalexin, terbinafine, and betamethasone, and he developed pain and swelling of the left tragus and ipsilateral cervical lymph nodes. He had no animal exposures, sports participation, immunodeficiency, or topical steroid use. On examination, he was afebrile and well-appearing. Vital signs were stable. Dermatologic examination revealed a 3 × 4 cm erythematous, scaly plaque on the frontal scalp with yellow, paste-like crusting and relative alopecia, and a tender, swollen left parotid region. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dL, white-blood-cell count of 13,700/mm3 with 70% neutrophils, an ESR of 25 mm/h, and a mildly elevated CRP. Urinalysis and cultures were negative. A potassium hydroxide preparation of hair and scalp scrapings was performed, and fungal culture was requested for definitive identification.
reasoning_trace:
1. Inflammatory tinea capitis favus was suspected because of the “distinct feature of thick, yellow crusts adhering to the scalp.”  
2. Non-inflammatory forms of tinea capitis were excluded given that “our patient experienced inflammatory lesions … erythematous lesions, scaly red plaques, and ultimately alopecia.”  
3. Pityriasis amiantacea was considered in the differential because “the differential diagnosis of inflammatory TC includes various conditions such as pityriasis amiantacea …”  
4. Bacterial folliculitis was considered as an alternative diagnosis: “ … bacterial folliculitis …”  
5. Impetigo was considered: “ … impetigo …”  
6. Pyoderma was considered: “ … pyoderma …”  
7. Pyogenic abscess was considered: “ … pyogenic abscess …”  
8. Erosive pustular dermatosis was considered: “ … erosive pustular dermatosis …”  
9. Pustular psoriasis was considered: “ … pustular psoriasis …”  
10. Langerhans cell histiocytosis was considered: “ … Langerhans cell histiocytosis …”  
11. Dissecting cellulitis was considered: “ … dissecting cellulitis …”  
12. Folliculitis decalvans was considered: “ … folliculitis decalvans.”

presentation: A 41-year-old man was admitted with worsening bilateral ear pain and three weeks of progressive hearing loss. He had no systemic symptoms of infection but noted a sensation of blocked ears. Initial examination revealed a perforated right tympanic membrane with purulent otorrhea and a red left tympanic membrane. Granulomatous ulcerations with clots and mucopurulent secretions were seen on the left nasal mucosa; the right nasal cavity was normal. White blood cell count was 11.62 × 10^3/uL with 64.7% neutrophils; C-reactive protein was 7.33 mg/L. Pure-tone audiometry showed symmetric severe mixed hearing loss in mid- and high-frequencies with a 40 dB air–bone gap. Impedance audiometry on the left was type B. Paracentesis yielded purulent fluid growing coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. Four days later, he developed bilateral tinnitus, worsening otalgia, headaches, facial numbness, and sudden bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy (House–Brackmann grade V). Repeat labs showed leukocytes 8.92 × 10^3/uL with 92.4% neutrophils and CRP 230 mg/L. Chest radiography was normal. Temporal bone CT demonstrated bilateral mastoid air-cell opacification, soft-tissue filling the tympanic cavities, and suspected erosion along the horizontal facial nerve canal on the right. Brain MRI confirmed bilateral mastoid inflammatory changes and marked mucosal thickening with fluid levels in multiple paranasal sinuses.
reasoning_trace:
1. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis was supported by necrotizing vasculitis on biopsy — “Focal acute inflammation of the arteries and veins with the fibrous necrosis of the walls was showed.”
2. c-ANCA positivity confirmed GPA over other vasculitides — “c-ANCAs are positive in about 80–90% of the cases.”
3. Chronic otitis media was considered but was unlikely given failure to improve with antibiotics and rapid progression — “Initially bilateral acute otitis media with purulent discharge from the right ear was diagnosed... antibiotic therapy was administered... Four days later, the patient's condition deteriorated significantly.”
4. Sarcoidosis was in the differential of granulomatous disease but was less consistent with necrotizing granulomas — “granulomatosis refers to necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.”
5. Polyarteritis nodosa was considered among systemic vasculitides but typically lacks granulomatous inflammation and upper airway involvement — “granulomatosis refers to necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, and polyangiitis concerns mainly small-diameter vessels.”
6. Tuberculosis was considered given granulomatous inflammation but was unlikely with a normal chest radiograph — “The chest X-ray showed lung fields without focal lesions and mediastinal margins within normal limits.”

presentation: A 27-year-old man, an average-built normotensive, non-diabetic, non-asthmatic policeman, presented with a 3-year history of post-meal chest tightness followed by vomiting. He experiences chest tightness 10–15 minutes after each meal, becomes restless in a pre-emetic phase, and then vomits undigested food in a non-projectile, non-bilious manner without blood or melena. His diet is normal and culturally appropriate. He is a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, and denies recreational drug use except a single unpleasant episode after cannabis. He has no history of headaches, aura, neurological symptoms, or family history of migraine. His sleep is disturbed and inadequate due to rotating day–night shifts. He consulted multiple specialists and underwent all routine and specialized investigations without contributory findings. He was hospitalized for further evaluation. During the stay, computed tomography of the abdomen and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were normal. Repeated mental-state examinations revealed anxiety but no diagnosable psychiatric disorder.
reasoning_trace:
1. Considered migraine because of reported associations with cyclic vomiting, but excluded because “there is no other history and symptoms supporting migraine.”  
2. Considered temporal lobe epilepsy due to episodic autonomic features, but excluded because “there are no other autonomic symptoms supporting temporal lobe epilepsy, and neuroimaging (MRI) revealed no abnormality.”  
3. Considered structural brain pathology, but excluded because “neuroimaging (MRI) revealed no abnormality.”

presentation:
A 32-year-old man with high-functioning autism spectrum disorder, depression, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented to the emergency department in the evening with restlessness and diffuse muscle stiffness. He described his legs as “stiff and heavy,” saying he “couldn't really move them,” and noted that his toes were intermittently turning inward with an unusual but not painful sensation. 

His home medications were losartan 100 mg daily, famotidine 20 mg daily, and sertraline 50 mg daily, which he had started 4 days earlier and had taken his fourth dose that morning. He denied use of any other medications, illicit substances, or supplements.

On examination, his heart rate was 61 bpm, blood pressure 164/94 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He had bilateral upper-extremity tremors, lateral ocular clonus on eye movement, and inducible clonus at the right ankle. Cranial nerves II through XII were intact; deep tendon reflexes were not documented.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel except for a potassium level of 3.3 mEq/L. Urine drug screen was negative. Thyroid-stimulating hormone level was normal. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with a QTc of 403 msec.
reasoning_trace:
1. Serotonin syndrome was confirmed by characteristic neuromuscular findings — “Patient was diagnosed with SS using Hunter's criteria given both inducible and ocular clonus, with restless agitation and tremor.”  
2. Anticholinergic toxicity was excluded based on the absence of anticholinergic medication use — “Other diagnoses (anticholinergic toxicity, …) were ruled out as the patient denied taking any other medications or antipsychotic, illicit substances, or supplements on the day of presentation to the ER or before.”  
3. Intoxication from sympathomimetic agents was excluded by a negative toxicology screen — “Urine drug screen was negative for any substances.”  
4. Withdrawal from sedative-hypnotic agents was excluded from the history and drug screen — “Other diagnoses (… withdrawal from sedative-hypnotic …) were ruled out as the patient denied taking any other medications or antipsychotic, illicit substances, or supplements on the day of presentation to the ER or before.”  
5. Thyroid storm was excluded by normal thyroid function testing — “Thyroid stimulating hormone level (TSH) … was normal.”  
6. Acute extrapyramidal syndromes were excluded by the lack of antipsychotic use and supportive history — “Other diagnoses (… acute extrapyramidal syndromes) were ruled out as the patient denied taking any other medications or antipsychotic, illicit substances, or supplements on the day of presentation to the ER or before.”

presentation:
A 61-year-old woman with a history of invasive lobular carcinoma of the right breast (T1N0) treated with mastectomy and adjuvant anastrozole presented in November 2017 for routine follow-up. In April 2015, she had developed bone metastases to T6, L2, and the sacrum, treated with radiotherapy, zoledronic acid, and a switch from anastrozole to letrozole. She reported no respiratory symptoms, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Thoracic CT revealed a new 1.5 cm×1.5 cm subpleural nodule in the left lower lobe with a broad base against the pleura. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated that the nodule was hypermetabolic (SUVmax 14.9) with an ill-defined border to the pleura; known vertebral lesions (eg, T6) remained FDG-avid (SUVmax 9.9). 

Laboratory studies showed normal lactate dehydrogenase and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with a mildly elevated β2-microglobulin (1.84 mg/L; normal 0.7–1.8 mg/L). Serologies for hepatitis B and C, HIV, and syphilis were negative. Bone marrow aspiration showed no malignant involvement.
ground_truth_diagnosis: Primary pulmonary diffuse large B cell lymphoma
reasoning_trace:
1. Lung metastasis of breast cancer — “In view of her history of breast cancer and multiple bone involvement, lung metastasis was considered (Figure 2).”  
2. Low-grade B-cell lymphoma (marginal zone or follicular lymphoma) — “no low-grade B-cell lymphoma components such as marginal zone lymphoma or follicular lymphoma were found around the tumor.”  
3. Mantle cell lymphoma — “blastic mantle cell lymphoma is immunoreactive to cyclin D1…in our patient…negative for Cyclin D1.”

presentation: A 60-year-old Caucasian woman with stage 5 chronic kidney disease presented with a 7-day history of heaviness and pain in the medial aspect of her left thigh. She denied fever, chills, or rigors. Her medical history included coronary artery disease, hypertension, well-controlled type II diabetes mellitus (HbA1C 5.6% six months earlier), and chronic kidney disease stage 5 (GFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m²). Medications were pioglitazone, furosemide, atenolol, lovastatin, lisinopril, isosorbide mononitrate, and metolazone. On examination, there was tenderness of the left thigh without edema or erythema; peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally. A Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities was negative for deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 13.1×10³/mm³, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, BUN 52 mmol/L, creatinine 4.7 mmol/L (baseline ∼5.0 mmol/L), calcium 10.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL, phosphorus 8.0 mg/dL, and PTH 2138 pg/mL (1381 pg/mL six months earlier). On hospital day 5, she developed peridermal necrotic areas with erythema and tenderness on the thigh. She was started on vancomycin for presumed cellulitis. However, the absence of fever and the markedly elevated PTH level prompted consideration of other causes. An x-ray of the thigh demonstrated extensive vascular calcifications.
reasoning_trace:
1. Deep venous thrombosis was considered but excluded — “A doppler ultrasound performed on bilateral lower extremities was negative for deep vein thrombosis.”  
2. Cellulitis was initially suspected but became unlikely — “She was initially started on vancomycin as the lesions were suspected to be secondary to local cellulitis. However the absence of fever and the presence of a markedly raised PTH levels along with the clinical picture of widespread necrosis with erythema made calciphylaxis a possibility.”  
3. Calciphylaxis rose to the top of the differential — “X-ray of left thigh was then obtained demonstrating extensive vascular calcifications … thus making calciphylaxis highly likely on our list of differential diagnosis.”

presentation: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 4 at 32 weeks of gestation, presented with repeated episodes of vaginal bleeding. On abdominal examination, the uterine fundal height was disproportionately large for her gestational age. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a single viable intrauterine fetus consistent with 32 weeks’ gestation. Screening of the adnexal regions showed bilateral complex masses with high vascularity measuring 8 × 6 cm on the right and 12 × 8 cm on the left. Transvaginal ultrasound identified a highly vascular polypoidal mass projecting into the upper vagina, indistinct from a bulky cervix, and solid peritoneal deposits in the pouch of Douglas. A non-contrast pelvic MRI performed one week later showed bilateral complex cystic adnexal masses and an upper vaginal mass on T2-weighted images. On diffusion-weighted imaging, these masses exhibited persistent bright signal intensity and low apparent diffusion coefficient values. Laboratory tests were within normal limits except for an elevated CA-125 level.
reasoning_trace:
1. Benign ovarian cysts and other common adnexal masses were considered but the presence of solid areas and increased Doppler flow favoured malignancy — “The presence of solid areas, as well as increased vascularity as determined by Doppler ultrasound, favoured the malignant nature of the lesions.”  
2. Diffusion-weighted MRI findings supported a malignant process rather than a benign lesion — “the masses showed restricted diffusion in the form of persistent bright signal intensity and low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values, which strongly favoured likely malignant pathology.”  
3. Heterotopic pregnancy was excluded because imaging confirmed only a single intrauterine gestation without extrauterine gestation — “Abdominal ultrasound examination showed a viable, single intrauterine 32 weeks fetus.”  
4. Primary vaginal cancer was deemed unlikely given its rarity compared with metastatic disease — “Although primary vaginal cancer is rare, metastatic disease to the vagina is not uncommon…”  
5. A primary cervical origin for the vaginal mass was excluded by MRI demonstration of uninvolved cervical margins — “MRI examination also showed free cervical margins, which was proven by histopathological examination in contrast to the ultrasound data.”
